newsitem.title: USA: U.S. supply of cattle on feed seen above year ago. [CORRECTED 21:37 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. supply of cattle on feed seen above year ago. [CORRECTED 21:37 GMT]

text.p: Profitable margins and sliding feed prices encouraged U.S. cattle feeders to keep placing cattle into feedlots in November and fed cattle numbers at major feedlots were projected to exceed last year's level, livestock analysts said.

The increased supplies are expected to be reflected by the U.S. Agriculture Department on Friday in its monthly Cattle on Feed report at 1400 CST/2000 GMT. A Reuter survey of analysts projected the data to show cattle on feed in lots of 1,000 head or more capacity in the seven key states Dec 1 at 103.2 percent of a year ago in a range of 102 to 104.2.
But November placements will be the key to the data, with pre-report estimates averaging 105 percent of a year ago, in a range of 98 to 110 percent.

"They were putting them (feeder cattle) on feed because they were making $85 to $100 a head on everything that was moving out of the feedlot so it gave them an incentive to put them back on feed," said Dale Benson, vice president and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
Benson also noted that grain prices continued to work lower through the month, which left plenty of incentive for cattle feeders to place cattle in feedyards.
However, not all analysts look for November placements to be sharply above the year-ago level.

"Though this year's (placement) number was pretty large, it was less than last year's number which was huge compared to the previous three years," said Dan Vaught, livestock analyst for AG Edwards. He estimated November placements at 98 percent of last year. (Corrects from 102 percent)

Vaught noted that placements were very large last year because of dry pastures, especially in Kansas and Texas, which forced owners to put lighter-weight cattle into feedlots. That was not the case this year with pastures in much better shape.
Marketing estimates for November were lower than year-earlier marketings, ranging from 91 to 98 percent and averaging 93.9 percent.

Part of the reason for the lower forecasts was that there was one less slaughter day this year than last in the month. Also, some heavy-weight cattle went from pastures straight to slaughter which trimmed the number of cattle sold by feedlots but counted in the total U.S. slaughter figures.

This is the 12th time the relatively new 12-state report will be released, but analysts continue to only estimate data for feedlots in the seven major cattle feeding states with capacities of 1,000 head or more as historical data continues to build.
